dataset_family: Hanyang University Hospitals (Seoul and Guri, Korea) sample, 32 MCI / 22 HC, 2022-2023
method_family: VR virtual-kiosk IADL behavioural biomarkers (HTC VIVE Pro Eye: hand speed, scanpath, time, errors) + T1 MRI volumetrics; SVM (unimodal and fused)
what_it_shows: A VR kiosk IADL task alone classified MCI vs HC at 88.9% accuracy (AUC 0.84) on a small held-out split. VR+MRI fusion reached 94.4%. An SVM on the SNSB-C battery, which also defines the labels, reached 94.4% as well, outperforming VR alone.
why: The PDF matches the block: Park et al., JMIR 2024;26:e54538; 54 participants (22 HC/32 MCI); VR kiosk + MRI; multimodal 94.4%. Read in full to the References. INSTRUMENT. The behavioural instrument is a virtual-kiosk IADL task scored on hand speed, scanpath length, completion time and errors. It runs on an HTC VIVE Pro Eye headset with integrated eye tracking, a hand controller, two base stations and a gaming laptop with an RTX 3080. This is commercially sold VR hardware, not clinical equipment, but it is a high-end rig. Whether it counts as 'consumer-grade' or 'without specialist hardware' is an operator call. It is not self-administered: the neurologists who made the diagnosis administered the test, after two practice sessions. MCI is a consensus diagnosis by two neurologists (Albert criteria, SNSB-C cut-offs). Participants were recruited at Hanyang University Hospitals in Seoul and Guri. VR-ONLY RESULT. Accuracy 88.9%, sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 90%, AUC 0.84, on a single 7:3 split (p.10, Table 5). This figure is not in the block, which reports only the VR+MRI 94.4%. WEAKNESSES. (a) The test set is tiny. The text says 16 of 54, but derived arithmetic points to 18: 87.5% sensitivity = 7/8, 90% specificity = 9/10, and the 88.9/94.4/83.3% accuracies are all multiples of 1/18. (b) The VR features were chosen by ANCOVA on all 54 participants before the split. (c) The 'best-performing' VR feature combination was picked among combinations evaluated on the same test set (Multimedia Appendix 2). Both (b) and (c) bias the figure upward. HEAD-TO-HEAD. This matters for the statement's second clause: the study does run a within-study head-to-head against a specialist instrument. An SVM on SNSB-C scores (RCFT, SVLT-E-DR), which the authors call 'a gold standard', reached 94.4%, against 88.9% for VR alone. The comparison is circular, because SNSB-C also defines the labels. Even so, admitting P-169 would make 'no head-to-head against a specialist instrument' false for the supporter set. AGAINST TABLE A1: behavioural yes; accuracy in the band yes (88.9%); consumer-grade arguable; self-administered no; 'no head-to-head' contradicted. Verdict: partly. AGAINST THE NARROWED WORDING: behavioural data with a best case of 88.9% in a small internally validated split fits. 'Without specialist hardware' is arguable for a VIVE Pro Eye rig. The wording's 'no head-to-head against a specialist instrument' is contradicted by the study's own SNSB-C comparison. Verdict: partly. INDEPENDENCE: a Korean hospital sample, distinct in dataset and method family from P-76/P-77 (I-CONECT facial video) and P-101 (Memory Guard). No authors are shared with the supporters or with the other candidates. Outside the supporter set, P-553 (EEG; Hanyang University Hospital outpatient memory clinic, Seoul and Guri; 12 MCI/13 HC) shares the recruitment site. It is neither a supporter nor a candidate. REGISTRY DEFECT: P-169's row gives Sample_N_Approx 22 (it should be 54) and Modality MRI/PET (the study is VR behavioural + MRI). The block's sample-size field also wrongly says 22.

quotes.quote: participants wore a head-mounted display with integrated eye-tracking capabilities (HTC VIVE Pro Eye) and used a hand controller in their dominant hand to select and order menu items from the virtual kiosk. Overall, 2 base stations tracked participants’ movements during the test.
a laptop equipped with an Intel i7-12700H processor, 16 GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 graphics card
The virtual kiosk test was administered by the same neurologists responsible for the MCI diagnosis
The 2 neurologists reached a consensus on the diagnosis of MCI based on the cutoff score of the Seoul Neuropsychological Screening Battery–Core (SNSB-C)
This study involved a total of 54 participants recruited from Hanyang University Hospitals in Seoul and Guri between January 2022 and July 2023.

Subsequently, the biomarkers that exhibited significant differences between the 2 groups were used to train and validate a multimodal learning model aimed at early screening for patients with MCI among healthy controls.

we used a train and test split with a ratio of 7:3, where 70% (38/54) of the participants were assigned to the train subcohort and the remaining 30% (16/54) of the participants were allocated to the test subcohort.

The best-performing SVM model using only VR-derived biomarkers, including hand movement speed, scanpath length, and the number of errors, achieved an accuracy of 88.9%, a sensitivity of 87.5%, a specificity of 90%, a precision of 87.5%, an F1-score of 87.5%, and an AUC of 0.84

the SVM model trained with SNSB-C data (RCFT and SVLT-E–DR), considered as a gold standard for MCI classification, exhibited strong performance, achieving an accuracy of 94.4%, a sensitivity of 100%, a specificity of 85.7%
VR-derived biomarkers align well with the requirements for a rapid screening tool in this phase, offering a brief testing duration (<5 min) with high specificity.
